title: Emerson forgetting
hookLine: in old age Emerson's memory faded; he forgot words but kept his gentleness

cards: A story people tell about Emerson in his last years. He wants to ask for his umbrella, and the word won't come. So he describes it instead: the thing that strangers take away.

A man who spent his life finding exactly the right word, reaching for an everyday one and missing it, and landing on something oddly lovely anyway. In his old age, Emerson's memory faded. Names slipped, then words.
In time the lectures and the writing fell away. And yet the people around him kept telling one more thing about those years.

teach.h: IT IS TIME TO BE OLD.
teach.b: First, he saw it coming. Some years before the fading, Emerson wrote a poem called Terminus, a word for a boundary stone. It opens, "It is time to be old," and speaks of taking in sail, like a ship coming into harbor.
It isn't a bitter poem. It reads like a man setting his affairs in order and choosing to be at peace with the tide. Second, the forgetting itself.

Another story people tell: at the funeral of a dear friend, the poet Longfellow, Emerson looked at the face for a long time and said, in effect, that he couldn't remember the name, but this had been a sweet and beautiful soul.

teach.h: THE NAME WAS GONE. THE LOVE WASN'T.
teach.b: The name was gone. The love wasn't. Third, what stayed.
Those who cared for him, his daughter Ellen among them, described a man still courteous, still smiling, still kind to visitors he could no longer place.

teach.h: THE WORDS WENT. THE MANNER STAYED.
teach.b: The words had gone; the manner remained. Fourth, why it matters here. This path has spent weeks with Emerson's mind.
His last years ask a quieter question: if the mind goes, what's left? In his case, the answer people remembered was gentleness.
Some traditions say, in their own way, that who a person is runs deeper than what a person remembers.
However you understand that, the old man forgetting the name and keeping the love is hard to forget.

how: Readers of Emerson often end with his late poem Terminus and the accounts of his final years, when his memory faded and those near him remembered his gentleness.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose memory is slipping, a grandparent, a neighbor, or simply someone who forgets your name, and picture them reaching for a word and missing it.
Now picture your face as they see it in that moment, and let it be patient and gentle: nothing to fix, just the face you'd want to meet if it were you.
